utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen, Your Honours. I fully understand the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances. You may sit down. Thank you and good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Patricia Sellers for the Office of the Prosecutor. With me today are co-counsel Gramsci di Fazio, Ms. Joanne Richardson and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry Frijlink. Good morning to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Sellers, and good morning to you and your reduced team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my friends from the OTP. My name is Vasvija Vidovic and together with John Jones I appearance for Naser Oric. We have with us our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic, and our CaseMap manager Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam, and good morning to you and your team. Before I give the floor to Mr. Jones, any preliminaries? None? Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Today I propose to deal with four broad subjects. The first is to answer Judge Brydensholt's question regarding who the guards were at the two locations and our position on that. Secondly, dealing with the opportunistic visitors to the prison and whether it was the guards or they who committed crimes in the two locations. Thirdly, I want to address the Prosecution's case as set out in the indictment and their case as it now emerges at the end of the trial and it's what I'll be referring to as the Prosecution's L, and we know what that means and I'll come back to that later. And then fourthly I'll be rejoining various points made by the Prosecution on Friday generally, just on a number of issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In order for us to plan the sitting, how much time do you anticipate you'll be?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I'm hoping I might be finished by the first break. That might be over-optimistic, but that's certainly possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, take your time. I'm just saying because otherwise I will -- I could give more time depending on how much time you require, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aiming for the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, as far as the first point is, the guards at the two locations, I'll use that as shorthand, we refer to the SUP and building, with a capital B, and the Prosecution refer to these two scenarios. But for the present purposes our case is that the Prosecution has not proved their allegation, their allegation that the military police were the guards at both locations. That's their allegation and they haven't proved it. We say that it was the civilian police who were the guards there, but of course that's not something which we have the burden of proving. Nonetheless, we are content to say that that's what the situation was. And it's paragraph 22 of the indictment where the Prosecution clearly made that allegation that the guards were military police, and I think there's no dispute at least about that allegation. Now, Ms. Richardson had two arguments essentially on Friday as to why they say the military police were the guards at the locations, and one was based on this Cude, Sabahudin Omerovic, and since the spelling is going to be important I think I should probably now make sure that's correct in the record. Yes, that's correct. And secondly what the accused said in his interview about Mirzet Halilovic. Now, neither of them are sustainable arguments. And actually first and foremost when we're considering the second location, the building, neither of those arguments apply to the second location, I think that needs to be absolutely clear, because there's no evidence relating to Cude at the second location. And Mirzet Halilovic died in January 1993, so equally that argument can't apply to the second location. So in my submission, firstly they have no arguments whatsoever for the military police being the guards at the second location. But let's go back to those two arguments in relation to the SUP. Now, what did -- who did Slavoljub Zikic say Cude was in fact when you look at his evidence? He said it was Sabahudin Omerovic, S-a-b-a-h-u-d-i-n Omerovic. And that's -- in fact, yes, we see the slide. It's 16 December 2004, T3346-3347, and I believe everyone has a hard copy of the slides, so obviously you can mark those up. "Question: And in fact one of the guards in the prison also knew you prior to your being kept prisoner there? "Answer: Yes. He knew me. He was a former police officer from Bratunac. His nickname was Cude. His last name was Omerovic and his first name was Sabahudin." And it's also on T3210, I'm not sure we have a slide on that, but he mentioned the same twice, Zikic, and each time he said Sabahudin Omerovic, and it's someone he knew before the war. Now, let's look at P590 which the Prosecution is linking this to where they say the name appears, and in fact it's Selahudin Omerovic. It's number 15, S-e-l-a-h-u-d-i-n. Now, the fact is, Your Honours, that's a different name in Bosnia, and it's as different as Alfred and Wilfred, even if they both end in Fred, and not only are they totally different names but you should recall that Mr. Zikic is a Bosnian. He's from Bosnia, and while we in the West might think the names are similar or might confuse them, he didn't. He knew this person from before the war. He mentions his name twice and each time he said Sabahudin. And in fact he knew him as a civilian policeman before the war as well, a policeman in Bratunac, and obviously before the war that would be a civilian policeman rather than military policeman. Now, Omerovic, as we've seen, is a very common name in that part of Bosnia. We've heard of at least three Omerovices: Hazim Mrki Omerovic; Safet Omerovic, Mis, and we even had a witness here Mensud Omerovic. There are Omerovices all over Srebrenica, and as you look through the exhibits you'll see that. Secondly, P590 also doesn't refer to Cude. At least if you had the nickname in common then you might think that the names were the same, but you don't even have the nickname Cude. And so, Your Honours, it would be a complete error to assume that Sabahudin Omerovic is the same person as Selahudin Omerovic without anything else to go on. I have a very good Bosnian friend who has two sons Amir and Emir, and how much of a mistake would it be to think that Amir Omerovic is the same person as Emir Omerovic. It would be a complete mistake, and there's only one letter difference. And in fact, our assistants, Adisa has a brother Adis; and our other assistant Jasmina has a brother Jasmin. It's actually quite common to give children names which are quite similar. So I don't know if Selahudin Omerovic is a brother of Sabahudin Omerovic, or his cousin, or absolutely no relation at all. All we do know is it's a different name, as different as Kevin Smith and Keith Smith, even though to Bosnian ears they may sound similar too. And also bear this in mind, Your Honours, that the Prosecution proofed Mr. Zikic, and they knew that their case was based on Zikic seeing that person in the prison. They could have known him P590, or they could have otherwise clarified when he testified whether it really was Sabahudin or someone of some other name but they didn't. So that argument simply does not work, the Cude argument. Moreover, there's evidence that Selahudin Omerovic, the person in P590, was in the civilian police, just like Nurija and just like Zele whom I'm coming to shortly, and that's D871, and you can see he's at number 24. And I would draw your attention to Nurija Jusufovic, number 3, and Elvir Djozic who we know is the one-armed policeman, Zele, at number 4. I'm going to come back to them. Now, interestingly the Prosecution want to rely in this case on P458 to show members of the military police. Well, you'll note that there's no Sabahudin Omerovic mentioned there. There is a Sabahudin Osmarovic at number 7 on page 3, and in fact only five names overlap between P458 and the list of military police there and P590, and I would just again emphasise the Prosecution's exhibits contradict each other. And, again, I think I made it clear on Friday, and I'll elaborate if I need to, but our position on Prosecution exhibits when we point ut these contradictions we're not relying on them. We're simply pointing out the contradictions in their exhibits, and if that's not clear I'm happy to clarify but I think -- I think Your Honours have understood. Right. Now, our case, as I say, is that the civilian police were the guards, and that's set out at paragraphs 532 to 545 of our final brief. And without superseding what's stated there we can present some of the evidence with slides, and it's important to do so because I think you'll finally begin to see the links between Becir Bogilovic, Nurija, Zele and the prisoners. So we can start with what I'm generally calling the evidence relating to the upstairs of the SUP. You'll recall that Becir Bogilovic's evidence that the military police were on the ground floor and the civilian police were on the first floor. It's not evidence we accept because we say they were mixed together. But if that's the case nonetheless, if the civilian police was on the first floor, and if it was being run from the first floor, then it's a reasonable assumption or inference that the guards who brought the prisoners up to the first floor for interrogation were civilian police. They were getting them from the cells, taking them upstairs for interrogation, and taking them back down again. And you'll see a pattern in the evidence. You'll see Ratko Nikolic first of all. Yes. "He took me out and took me upstairs at the police station. There was a man sitting there and there was a pistol and a knife there on the table." Upstairs at the police station. Zikic: "On another occasion, I went to the first floor, because this was on the ground floor, so this time I went to the first floor, where the questioning was conducted by the police." So again, this would be the civilian police conducting questioning. And then on P98. This was Sarac speaking. "Then they called me for an interrogation upstairs to Mirza ... He is head of the SUP." Now, if that's a reference to Mirzet Halilovic, you'll see that although he is the military police commander, he's there on the first floor where the civilian police are which just goes to show that the military police and the civilian police were mixed together and that Mirzet Halilovic as we know was the subordinate of Becir Bogilovic. But I'll return to that too. So you have all that evidence of actually people being brought upstairs for interrogation, and I submit that's evidence that the civilian police were the guards and that they were running the show. Then if we consider Nurija. And Nurija Jusufovic is terribly important when one comes to the SUP. You'll recall that Nurija Jusufovic was the civilian police chief and his fingerprints, figuratively speaking, are all over the SUP and all over the building and all over the prisoners. And you'll see that addressed at paragraphs 537 to 540 of our closing brief. He was involved in providing blankets to detainees in the second location, in refurbishing the premises at the second location. And he's linked to -- linked to both places, as is Zele. Now, if we look at what Ivanovic said, and this is when he was brought to the SUP. I won't read the dates since it's on the record with the slides. But Ivanovic said: "Nurija was standing in the hallway of the police station," this is when Ivanovic arrived at the SUP, "And he asked me, Chetnik, do you know Pero Milosevic," et cetera, and he was subjected to verbal abuse by Nurija. "And after he said this to you, did he ask you any questions about yourself or anything else for that matter? "After that they seized my wallet." And that includes all these identification details and documents. "They made some remarks and then took me along to the cell to the right of the entrance to the police station." And we have bean to that location and we know very well that's exactly where the cells are as you go in to the right. "Once I was just outside the cell they opened the door. One of them kicked me in the small of my back, and I banged my head against a radiator." Now, I can't emphasise strongly enough the significance of that evidence. This is the civilian police chief receiving a Serb detainee in the SUP, taking his documents from him, taking him or at least his people, Nurija's people taking him to the cell and being the first to mistreat him as well, kicking him into the cell. It shows that the civilian police were dealing with the detention of Serb prisoners and that in fact they were even the ones mistreating them. And then if we looked at P475, and this relates to the people who were held in the second location, the building. This is the list of detainees which -- which Mr. Ivanovic gave evidence about. And you see there: "Not knowing whether Nurija was the SUP commander." And again, this is a list put together by someone who had been in detention in the second location and who had come across Nurija and was wondering what his position was. And as I say, that is -- that was his position. He was the head of the civilian police and a subordinate of Becir Bogilovic. And that's dealt with at paragraph 540 of our closing brief. And then if we look at D987, and D866, that deals with the prisoners from Karno. And these are Serb prisoners in respect of whom we have this note from Nurija Jusufovic: "Avdic, I have here imprisoned the Serb citizens from Karno, nine of them. They were brought in during last night and they are now here. Please decide and tell us what to do with these citizens." So this is Nurija Jusufovic, civilian police chief, asking the president of the War Presidency, a civilian body, what to do with detained Serbs. And there's no reason in my submission why the Karno Serbs should be any different from any of the other Serb detainees. This was -- these were the people dealing with Serb detainees as the evidence shows. And then if we see D871 again, you will see there, as I said, Nurija Jusufovic on list and Zele and Selahudin Omerovic as members of the civilian police. Now, when we turn to the next general heading, sub-heading within this -- this subject, uniforms, the detainees themselves testified that they were held by either civilian police or people in civilian uniforms. Radic said: "And this was, as far as you could tell, a civilian police operation, wasn't it? You were in the civilian SUP, and it was the civilian police who were questioning you. "Answer: Yes." And Mr. Ivanovic: "Once there, there were police officers who were wearing blue uniforms, the kind they used to wear in the former Yugoslavia." Those blue uniforms are civilian police uniforms. And then Nikolic, and this was referring to the second location, said in response to the question: " ... the guards... They were civilian police, weren't they ... Yes, yes." The Prosecution tried to suggest in their response that maybe Mr. Nikolic was confused by the question because I put to him a question, as far as you could tell, this was the civilian police, if you saw that or heard, and he said yes. Well, if there was any confusion the Prosecution could have objected or they could have clarified the matter in re-examination, and they didn't. So there's no disputing that answer which he gave. And then when we consider Zele, Elvir Djozic, in my submission it becomes very interesting and very revealing. Ms. Richardson said that Branko Mitrovic never said Zele was at the prison. Well, in fact, Mr. Mitrovic said that Zele took him from the SUP to a flat. So he obviously was at the SUP because he went in, took Branko Mitrovic and took him out. And not only that, but if you read Branko Mitrovic's evidence carefully he then took Mr. -- took Branko, as I'll call him, took him to the second location as well, and he took him every day. So you have Zele, civilian policeman, takes a Serb detainee out of the SUP and then he's taking him to the second location every day. What does that tell you about who is running the detention of Serb prisoners? Obviously the civilian police. It's the best proof that the -- well, not the best proof but it's one of many good proofs that detainees were held by the civilian police, because otherwise how could a civilian policeman just drift into the SUP, take a boy out who is a detainee and then take him to another location and just come and go as he pleases with detainees if it's nothing to do him? And in my submission it's obvious that the detainees were held by the civilian police, and if at least you don't consider it obvious then certainly it raises a reasonable doubt that the military police were the guards. We'll see that slide now for Branko. And he's talking about where he was taken to the flat in Kazani, and he describes there how he spent a night there and there was a lady cook which also fits with Svetlana Trifunovic's first statement, not her evidence but her first statement to Behara: "I seem to remember that they referred to that person as Zele, as counsel suggested a while ago. It's coming to me gradually. It does ring a bell definitely." And if -- if you give me a moment. Yes, D871 we've seen already. Then if we look at the evidence of Mr. Guster about the exchange of C007. Now, Ms. Richardson tried to suggest that Guster's evidence was simply that Zele was just there during the exchange, he was just present as were lots of other people. Not at all. He was actively involved running the show one might even say. And you can see that from Guster's testimony: "You told us earlier that you saw the man without an arm who went in the direction of that house." And that house as we know refers to the building where the Serb detains were kept. So he was actually going in the direction and then he shows up again. "This person without an arm, wearing civilian clothes, who had come out of that house, came to us and told us that the APC had left for Zvornik and not for Tuzla." So, in other words, he's gone no the house, he's come out. In our submission, he's taken out C007, and then he confirms that when they tried to find out who he was: "The people who were close by addressed him by the name of Zele and told us that Zele was a policeman." So we know that that's Zele who is going in and out of the building and essentially evacuating C007. And then we see on the next slide he was shown a photograph, Mr. Guster. "This is the man without the arm. At the time I saw him, he did not have a uniform; he was wearing civilian clothes." You will recall he had a uniform in the video because he'd just lost his arm in action.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "That's the man who was with the UNPROFOR men on that day." So he was with the blue helmets. He wasn't simply standing around. He was in the interlocutor for the UNPROFOR in achieving the evacuation of C007. And you'll recall that the other person who is very actively involved in that day was Mr. Nekic who was member of the War Presidency. And again this reinforces that it was a civilian operation, War Presidency, civilian police, liaising with Morillon and evacuating C007. Now, when we turn to Becir Bogilovic, he himself admitted that he supervised the work of Nurija at the SUP. I think we have a slide on that. Yes. And there it is. And this is -- we're talking about August, September, October 1992, precisely when the detainees were in the SUP. And he says -- he conceded that he overseed -- oversaw the work of Nurija Jusufovic at the SUP building and on most occasions Nurija would come and see him. So he's is supervising the work of Nurija, and Nurija was the one who received Ivanovic and kicked him into his cell. So Becir Bogilovic is directly linked and implicated in the detention of Serbs. And Zele, he admitted, was a policeman of his. We can see that in the next slide. " ... during your testimony, you mention a policeman of yours and you said his number was Zele. Is this Elvir Djozic? "Yes. "At one point he was wounded and lost an arm. Is that the same person? "Yes, it is." So Zele, who is taking Branko out of the SUP, who is helping with the evacuation of C007, who is taking Branko to the second location, is a policeman of Becir Bogilovic's. He's -- Becir Bogilovic's is implicated through Nurija and through Zele in the detention of Serbs. Now we get to the evidence of Mr. Bogilovic who said that the civilian police did not detain prisoners. Now, Mr. Bogilovic had every reason, you can see from this, he had every reason to distance himself from the detention of Serbs and because otherwise he himself might be in the dock for murder and cruel treatment. And he was warned repeatedly by Your Honour for being evasive, for not telling the truth. He was not a credible witness. And I submit the reason why he was so evasive is that he was very concerned for his own skin. And I refer to what we said about his credibility in paragraphs 658 to 660 of our closing brief. And so this self-serving explanation of a non-credible witness in my submission is of no probative value, and it is completely contradicted by the evidence which we've been reviewing and which we'll continue to review, and it's in complete contradiction with all the evidence that he was the superior of Mirzet Halilovic, because if Mirzet Halilovic is in charge of Serb detainees, then obviously Becir was too as his superior. And let's look at what Becir Bogilovic said when he was asked about this, and it's T6249. And I submit you can see the evasiveness in his very answer. Question: "Mr. Bogilovic, when you went to the MUP or SUP building in the month of September or October, did you ever see Serb prisoners on the ground floor of the building? "No. No, no. I would get in and I would pass through. I did not go there very often, but I would always go straight upstairs, precisely because of him. "And when you say 'him,' are you referring to Mr. Halilovic? "I mean Mr. Halilovic. I mean, talk about wilful blindness. Here you have a man whose subordinate is Mirzet Halilovic, and according to him he's running up the stairs so he couldn't see what's going on on the ground floor. But in my submission he'll in all likelihood run into Mirzet Halilovic upstairs because as we've seen Mirzet was already interrogating people on the first floor. I'm not saying on that day but in all probability he's going to run into Mirzet Halilovic sooner or later, and he is no doubt going to run into Mirzet Halilovic when Mirzet Halilovic would bring his reports to him, and when he and Mirzet Halilovic would both report to Hajrudin Avdic. So far from being able to avoid his subordinate, Mirzet Halilovic. He would be see him all the time at the SUP and when -- when receiving his reports. Now, despite all of the above, Ms. Richardson said on Friday there is absolutely no evidence, absolutely no evidence, she said, that the civilian police were involved in the prison either during the first prison scenario or during the second. There was no evidence that Hajrudin Avdic, the president of the War Presidency was there, Bogilovic, or Jusufovic. Well, Jusufovic I've already dealt with. Hajrudin Avdic is not a civilian policeman; he's the president of the War Presidency. So I don't see why they think it's necessary for him to be physically present manhandling prisoners or otherwise at the SUP. There is, however, abundant evidence of his involvement with the prisons and prisoners as set out in our closing brief, and there's the matter of refurbishing the second location. There's also, if we see P45. Yes, P45. And there we have a document headed War Presidency, and it's the list of prisoners and deceased persons being offered for exchange. And it's all the victims in the indictment: Jakov Djoric, Branko Sekulic, Dragan Lilic, et cetera. So far from being absolutely no evidence, there's abundant evidence that the War Presidency was involved with the detention of Serbs. And this is a Prosecution exhibit. It's interesting that the Prosecution now say there is absolutely no evidence that Bogilovic was ever in the prison. In their final brief they state, this is paragraph 399: "The prisoners recalled interactions with Becir Bogilovic," according to the Prosecution. At paragraph 405 of their closing brief it says: "In addition to his interrogation by Mirzet Halilovic" -- this is referring to Zigic -- sorry, Radic, at which time his teeth were knocked out, "Slavoljub Zikic was interrogated by the former police commander of Srebrenica who sat on the first floor of the SUP building. While the former police commander did not identify himself to Zikic, the Trial Chamber has heard evidence from Becir Bogilovic that he was the former police commander in Srebrenica and his officers were on the first floor of the Srebrenica SUP building above the ground floor space used by the military police. Bogilovic made it clear to Slavoljub Zikic that he knew Zikic from before and recognise him." So I simply don't understand what the Prosecution's case is as far as Becir Bogilovic is concerned. Do they say that he was never in the SUP, or do they say that he was there doing what he was doing? I suppose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, what's the problem Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I don't want to mislead Defence counsel. The first cite that he went to in terms of Bogilovic being in the prison, that was among the errors the Prosecution made in its closing brief. And the second one is just interpretation. We're not saying it was an error. It's the interpretation the Defence has given it now. But I don't want to mislead the Defence on that evidence

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Ms. Sellers. Yes, Mr. Jones. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I rather wish the Prosecution had pointed that out earlier. We know it's a mistake, but it would have been proper to correct that a long time ago, particularly as we pointed it out in our response. In any event, there's not just a reasonable doubt that the military police detained prisoners. In fact, all the evidence, all the credible evidence, and I leave aside the self-serving evidence of Becir Bogilovic, points the other way. Now, as far as the interview, the suspect interview is concerned, Ms. Richardson also relies on the interview where the accused apparently said Mirzet Halilovic was in charge of prisoners. Now, I've already made a point that doesn't apply to the second location. Just concentrating on the first location, I'll say this: I want to preface what I'll say about this with the following though. You will recall how -- how withering Mr. di Fazio was about the interview on -- on Friday, how disappointed he was by the fact that it wasn't a confession. But then you'll recall how many times the Prosecution then refer to the interview. And we counted. They referred to the interview 82 times in their closing brief, 68 times in their response, and then even after Mr. di Fazio said how the interview really wasn't much use at all, they referred to his interview another five times. And they're forever citing the interview, and in fact it increasingly looks like the whole case is built on the interview. It's strange, therefore, that they say it's a self-serving interview, but they say that, of course, because they wish to deprive our client of any credit for giving an interview. And what's self-serving is how the Prosecution use his interview while denying it's of any use to them. But anyway, on the interview, there are three points I would make. Firstly there is no indication of the time period. I mean, there never is in the interview. You don't know what period the accused is talking about when he made that statement. And our other points on the interview remain. You don't know whether it's something someone told him years later or whether it's actually the fruit of his own recollection. But secondly, Your Honour Judge Brydensholt's question was about the guards who were the guards. And even if Mirzet Halilovic were in charge of the detainees, it doesn't actually say anything about who the actual guards were who were actually taking care of the prisoners, because you'll recall the evidence that people were being taken upstairs, so the point remains that civilian police could be actually the ones who were dealing with the detainees. And that's what we're interested in, whether they were the ones mistreating the detainees or allowing others to mistreat them. It's their affiliation which is important. And whether Mirzet Halilovic was in charge or not doesn't say anything about who were the actual guards. That remains an open question. You'll recall all the evidence of how the military police was within the civilian police. There's abundant evidence on that, and it's set out in our brief, and of how Mirzet Halilovic reported to be Becir Bogilovic. So if Mirzet Halilovic was in charge of prisoners, it doesn't provide evidence in relation to the affiliation of the guards coming and going. And the proof of that, if that seems at all controversial, is that if it did, let's assume that Mirzet Halilovic being in charge of the prisoners means that any guards, the military police, well, that would lead you to assume, wouldn't it, that Zele must be military police. That would lead you to assume that Nurija is military police. But those assumptions would both be wrong and that proves that in fact that's no answer to the question of who the guards were. The Prosecution cited paragraph 114 of Blaskic on uniforms and their affiliations of persons. I don't think that will assist Your Honours at all that section. Firstly it's actually to do with victims, that passage. But secondly one can envisage a scenario where there are regular soldiers who have uniforms and then they take their uniforms off and they're in other clothes when they commit some crime and they remain liable as members of the unit. I think that's probably the gist of the Prosecution's submission. But that doesn't help you at all to work out someone who is in civilian clothes what his affiliation is. And they're saying if he's military police, the fact that he's in civilian clothes couldn't change that affiliation, but they haven't proved that he's military police anyway, so it doesn't even get you anywhere. Now that responds, I believe, to Your Honour Judge Brydensholt's question. But, Your Honours, while I'm on the subject of the detention charges there are a couple of points I have to clarify. On Friday

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON SAID
utterances.text: "Mr. Jones referred to Ilija Ivanovic's identification of the accused in the reception room while he was imprisoned in Srebrenica. And Mr. Jones stated that Ratko Nikolic did not state that he saw Naser Oric, and it would seem strange that if they were both there together, then Ratko Nikolic would have mentioned this, she says, and that's a valid point if it were true. And I'm glad Ms. Richardson concedes that it would be a valid point. At least we agree on something. Because it is true, and I'll show you why it's true in a moment. She said: "Mr. Ivanovic never at any time," she was completely emphatic on this, "never at any time contrary to the Defence stated that Ratko Nikolic was present." It's a pity she was so emphatic because it is in fact completely true. Nikolic was in the room with Ivanovic. And to see that it's true all you have to do is take our closing brief and go to paragraph 330 where we made that point. It's not difficult. And there we said Ivanovic testified that on one occasion he was taken with Nikolic and Pejic to a reception room in the building where there were five men. And we very helpfully provided a footnote. And we didn't only put the transcript reference, we actually quoted it. And it was my question: "Just sticking with the meeting in the reception room, was it right that Ratko Nikolic was there at the same time as you when you were brought into see the five men? Answer: Yes, that's correct. Rade Pejic and Ratko Nikolic were there." So it's absolutely crystal clear. It was plain for everyone to see, including the Prosecution if they read the closing brief thoroughly. The page that Ms. Richardson referred to is simply Ivanovic saying, "I was taken from my cell and taken to a reception room." He didn't say, "No one else was taken with me." And that was clarified later that he was there with Nikolic. So, as I say, I'm glad that it's conceded to be a valid point and it has the great virtue of also being true. And Nikolic's presence is key. It's absolutely key. Because he had seen Naser Oric before being in the prison when he was in Kravica and then he never saw him again. So if Naser Oric was there in the reception room a few feet away from him when Ivanovic was there, Nikolic would have said, yes, I did see Oric again in the reception room. Whereas in fact what he did -- what in fact Nikolic said is - we can see the next slide - "After your capture on the 12th of January, 1993, did the man that you knew as Naser Oric, did you ever see him again? "No. "And you were exchanged on the 27th of February -- "Yes." So he didn't see him between the 12th of January and the 27th of February. Now, that -- that in my submission is the final nail in the coffin of any motion that Ivanovic saw Naser Oric in the reception room, even without all the uncertainties expressed by Ivanovic about on that point. And now Your Honours I move to my next global category of submissions. It was made clear on Friday that our client is not being held responsible for the acts of opportunistic visitors or for others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, Judge Eser would like to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I just would like to ask you, because I'm not acquainted with the term "opportunistic visitors." Now, is it a term of art or was it an invention to express certain things? What is the difference between opportunistic visitors and civilians or other visitors? What is it about opportunistic about visitors?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. It is an expression which is used in the case law. It's been invoked once or twice. And the notion of opportunistic visitors, I think, is those of who see an opportunity to get in somewhere where they don't belong, and they sneak in through a door or they break in. In other words, they take advantage of an opportunity to enter someone where they don't normally belong. Whereas if you spoke of visitors, a visitor could be someone who actually is perfectly entitled to be there. So it suggests the notion of people who shouldn't be there but who manage to get in. For the purposes of today's submissions, it might be easier if I simply say others, because later some of the slides I just use others, others being distinct from guards, and I'm happy just to use that term, or third persons. And, yes, so in our submission, these others, their acts are not attributable to our client, and so we only have to deal with the guards and what the guards did. And there's ample evidence that the guards were not the ones who did beatings and did -- and committed murder. And if we look quickly at the slides we have there, we have for the SUP. It's paragraph 489 of our closing brief. The perpetrators of beatings were not the guards at the SUP but people who came from outside. And you can see Ivanovic. "I couldn't really say that it was the guards who beat us because if they had beat us, they have probably opened the door, whereas the people who did beat us would do it through the bars." And Ivanovic also said at T4181: "I did say clearly that they did not come into the cell." The perpetrators. Nikolic confirmed that the people who beat him were not the guards but people who came from outside the prison. And he again made this point that the beating was through the bars. And he also testified that on one occasion, I think this might have been at the second location, but guards even tried to prevent him being beaten. Then when we turn to the second location, it's at paragraphs 490 to 493 of our closing brief and all the footnote references. But we see there Nikolic at T2721: "As far as who you beat you, Mr. Nikolic, in the prison, isn't right that it wasn't the guards who did it but people who broke into the prison ... broke into the prison to, as you put it, see the Chetniks. It was those people from outside who beat you. "Yes. And Ivanovic at T4042: "As I've already said, the beatings would start after dusk, at 9.00 or 10.00 in the evening. When the soldiers would return from the battlefield they would be driven in a truck, stop between the court and the police station in the municipality building, then they would say let's go and see the Chetniks, and they would beat us in any way they could with whatever implements they had." So these are not guards. These are people coming from outside. And what's also very interesting is his evidence that this happened at night, after dusk. And you'll recall that Radic also said: "During the day we were left alone, no one touched us, it was at night that we were beaten." And I've pointed out before the evidential void in knowing how people got into the SUP and the building. But imagine even that simply the guards weren't there in the evening. It's not -- it's not an incredible suggestion. That perhaps they simply went home and that's when these people broke in and beat them. It's obviously -- it's not -- not great behaviour on their part and not terribly responsible to just leave detainees in the evenings. But at the same time, if we're talking about whether the guards had a murderous mens rea, whether they intended that the detainees would be cruelly treated and murdered, then going home at the end of the shift and -- and not taking enough care about the detainees does not reach that level. But as I said, it's all speculation because we simply don't know how people got into the two locations. C007 was mostly beaten by an unidentified Muslim in civilian clothes who had just been released from custody from the Serbs in Bratunac and who in our submission is -- is -- was certainly not identified as a guard. Mico was actually killed by some young man - at one point he even conceded he might have been 16 years old - who again somehow got into the prison but was not a guard. And so since the Prosecution has made clear that they don't hold the accused responsible for acts of these others, in our submission that should be an end of it. He's entitled to an acquittal on that basis and on that basis alone. Now, as we know, the Prosecution has, I would say, a new theory now, a new theory, completely new in fact, which only emerged when they responded to our closing brief. And I want -- I think this -- this is a matter which should be crystal clear, and I want to make sure it's crystal clear, and so rather than having the triangle chart, I've got two charts now, and the first will show the Prosecution's case as set out in the indictment, and you can see it on the chart. And it's what I'm calling vertical liability only. It's Article 7(3) liability, superior, subordinate, and the subordinates were the guards and the others. That was their case. That all the people who were involved in murdering or beating the detainees were subordinates of the accused. That's the case we had to meet. And we knew that they couldn't prove that all these people were subordinates of the accused. And that was their case and so they changed their case once that emerged, and so we now have this new version. We can see on the next slide. I'm calling that the Prosecution's case after the close of the trial, as set out in its response to the Defence closing brief. And so this is the L. It's a vertical responsibility to which has now been added a horizontal responsibility, an extra level of aiding and abetting between the subordinates and the others. And as I said on Thursday, I believe it was, yes, it's ultra vires the Statute, that argument. It wasn't pleaded and it hasn't been proved. And I spoke at great length on that subject, and I don't plan to revisit all of those submissions, but I do plan to revisit the submission that the indictment does not set out that L case. The indictment sets out the vertical case only, and I want to emphasise that. Your Honour Judge Eser asked last week or made the point that our client was not being held responsible for the acts of these others directly on this dotted line which would be the hypotenuse of the triangle. But that we were always clear on because of course under Article 7(3) you can't hold the accused directly responsible for non-subordinates. That's just simply the law that's no comfort to us whatsoever to be told that. What we're complaining of is precisely this L. That's what ultra vires, not pleaded and not proved. Now, I'd like to come at it this way by starting with some -- one extract of case law. It's in the Kupreskic appeals judgement, and it's cited, regularly cited on this point. That the Appeals Chamber said, and it's 23rd of October, 2001: "The Appeals Chamber emphasizes that the Prosecution is expected to know its case before it goes to trial. It is not acceptable for the Prosecution to omit the material aspects of its main allegations in the indictment with the aim of moulding the case against the accused in the course of the trial depending on how the evidence unfolds." Now the Prosecution have been repeatedly stating, Oh, no, our case is based on aiding and abetting. That's perfectly clear. If it were clear, the indictment would have said under the detention charges we're running aiding and abetting. They would use the words "aiding and abetting," they would invoke Article 7(1), we would know that was their case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, Defence counsel. Just two issues. I don't know whether this is law that Defence counsel would wish to pass up to us prior to using today. That's one issue. And the other is just to make sure that the Trial Chamber again isn't misled in terms of the 7(1) argument that I think we tried to clarify with the Defence last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, two points really. The first -- there's maybe even a slight point of order in that this is our rejoinder to their rebuttal. The Prosecution is not going to be responding, as I understand, to our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, of course not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's a different submission from last Friday when we were going to have to respond off the cuff and we wanted to have authority so we could do so, and the Prosecution isn't going to be responding, so they're in a different situation altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Plus we are dealing with -- with a principle that that governs all criminal proceedings everywhere, that this is why you have an indictment in the first place. I mean, you're supposed to know exactly what your case -- case rests upon. And in our case before an indictment is confirmed you have this supporting documents in any case, and that's what basically the whole case is supposed to be based upon. And then after that of course it is built up. It's beefed up, and in these cases, these type of cases, information is arriving as a matter of fact even throughout the course of a case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And if I may just respond to that, it's true that facts emerge and every fact under the sun emerges during the trial, but the fact -- given that facts emerge, that doesn't mean that we at that moment become -- that we're then on notice that this is become part of the Prosecution's case, and that's why there's the distinction the indictment has to set out the case. So I turn to the indictment and paragraph 22 of the indictment. We can see that on our -- on the monitor. So this is what they were saying the Prosecution, paragraph 22: "Between 24 September 1992 and 20 March 1993, members of the military police under the command and control of Naser Oric detained several Serb individuals in the Srebrenica police station and in the building behind the Srebrenica municipal building." So that's stage 1, the military police are the guards. We've addressed that. Then paragraph 23 deals with perpetrators. And I won't read the whole thing. You can see it there. But the key -- key passage is the first: "These detainees were subjected to physical abuse, serious suffering and serious injury to body and health, and inhumane treatment by the guards and/or by others with the support of the guards." So there we have who the perpetrators are. Guards and these others. And then we go to paragraph 26: "Naser Oric," from those dates, "knew or had reason to know that his subordinates were about to plan, prepare, or execute the imprisonment, killing, and/or cruel treatment of Serbs detained at the" -- the two locations. So that's -- and then that leads into the actual charges. So that's absolutely clear. The subordinates are the guards and the others. The guards and the others who have been spoken of in paragraph 23 are then subsumed under subordinates in paragraph 26. And that's why it's a vertical responsibility. Their case was that Naser Oric was the superior of the guards and the others who mistreated detainees. And that's our understanding of what their case was and it's the case which we addressed. Now if there are any doubts, look at paragraph 39 of the Prosecution's response to our motion on the form of the indictment for June 2003, and this is the Prosecution speaking: "The Defence objection under this heading is misconceived." Is one of our objections. "The Prosecution does not allege criminal liability of the accused merely on the ground that his subordinates were about to plan and/or prepare. The accused's criminal responsibility alleged under paragraph 26," that's the paragraph we just saw, "is his failure to prevent the commission of alleged crimes by his subordinates and/or his failure to punish such subordinates who committed crimes alleged in the indictment." And so there it is clear beyond a shadow of a doubt that the Prosecution's case was based on subordinates of the accused committing crimes, that the guards and the others beat and killed detainees, and they are subordinates of the accused. That was their case. Now, we know the Prosecution, and it emerged during the course of the trial the Prosecution couldn't prove that. They can't prove that the young man who killed Mico, allegedly killed Mico was a subordinate. They can't prove those people who jumped out a truck and said, Let's get the Chetniks, they can't prove that their Oric's subordinates. And Your Honours knew that, too, because you pointed out at the close of the Prosecution case that these others were -- had never been identified. We have Kemo, and I want to just have one digression on Kemo who might otherwise be considered a special case. I want Your Honours to bear in mind that only Radic referred to Kemo from Pale. Zikic referred to a Beli who we also thought was from Pale. Beli from Pale was a guard as someone he referred to. And one thing also which will be striking for Your Honours is that Radic talked about Kemo. Nedret Mujkanovic talked about Kemo. Hakija Meholjic talked about Kemo. Were we ever shown a photograph of Kemo so that you could at least have some comfort level in knowing that this was the same Kemo, or actually saying to Mr. Radic, "Is this the Kemo you saw?" And then showing it to Hakija and to Dr. Mujkanovic and then confirming, so at least you would know that they were on the same wavelength. Whereas what might have happened is you show a photograph to one of them and the other says, "No, no that's not the man at all." That was never done, and you think for murder as a war crime that's something which would have been entitled to see. Kemal is a very common name in that area, and we have all the confusion about Ahmetovic and Mehmetovic. I also just want to mention on the subject that these names, Your Honours may or may not know, but Beli means a lot, a light man, light -- white or light man; Mrki means dark, dark man. These are very vague nicknames people have who been have identified by, and certainly with Kemo we would certainly not concede for a moment that it's clear that he was the person who killed Kukic. There's a reasonable doubt that the Kemal mentioned there is Kemo Mehmetovic. But in any event, we also say that the evidence does not prove at all that Kemo was a subordinate of Oric. So the case, the Prosecution's case falls flat. They don't have any subordinate of Oric who actually beat or killed a detainee. So now they change and they come up with this new theory. Well, Your Honours, we made all our decisions about what case to present, what witnesses to call, what questions to ask based on the idea or based on the Prosecution's case that the others were subordinates of Naser Oric. And if we had notice of a different case, we could have called witnesses, for example, to rebut the aiding and abetting theory. And you'll even note, Your Honour, I don't want to get into specifics, but in our 65 ter witness summaries we had a Medsid Djozic [phoen], for example, and I'm not going to say what we propose to call him for, but I'll just say this. That we certainly could have called witnesses who could have come here and who could have said actually the guards were not aiding and abetting at all. They were trying to stop or -- there are all sorts of approaches we would have taken if it ever -- if we ever dreamt that the Prosecution was going to say the guards aided and abetted others to commit crimes and that's where your client's responsibility derives from. We would have -- the whole tenor of our case would have been different. So, Your Honours, if this new theory is adopted at the eleventh hour, our client would be tried and convicted on a theory which he never had notice of. The pre-trial brief also made it clear that the Prosecution alleged that it was subordinates of the accused themselves who physically murdered and cruelly treated detainees. And I submit that's actually crystal clear from the pre-trial brief too. Now, paragraph 51 the Prosecution set out the elements that they would have to prove for murder. And you'll note that they set out the mens rea, you see the elements there A, B and C. But C, the accused or a subordinate of the accused must have intended to kill or inflict serious injury and reckless disregard of human life. Now that's the mens rea of a physical perpetrator, the person who was actually doing it. The mens rea for aiding and abetting is quite different and you'll know it's quite different because in paragraph 97 of the pre-trial brief the Prosecution set out the mens rea for aiding and abetting which they were going to rely on for the wanton destruction charges. Now if they thought at all at that stage that they were going to be using aiding and abetting for the detention charges, they would have set out the mens rea for aiding and abetting, but they didn't because their case was that the subordinates of the accused killed, physically killed and inflicted serious injury, not that they aided and abetted someone else to do so. Now look at paragraph 154 of the pre-trial brief. "Naser Oric failed to issue orders as a reasonable -- as a reasonable measure to prevent troops under his command from destroying and plundering." That's the wanton destruction. But then at the bottom: "Naser Oric also failed to issue orders to prevent his subordinates from murdering or cruelly treating Serbian detainees," held in those two locations. So, again, it's clear there, the idea is that his subordinates were murdering or cruelly treating, persons under his effective control, not people jumping out of lorries and mistreating the detainees. It's a completely different case and they're doing a U-turn after all the evidence is in. Now, Your Honours, I hope that that's sufficiently clear, our position on that. I can certainly address it in more detail, if need be, but those are -- those are -- that's what I would say on that subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's clear enough for the three of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Because I'll move to a new subject then, Your Honour, which is addressing some of the points in rebuttal, so a completely new area. So levee en masse, I just have a couple of rebuttal points. In discussing levee, the Prosecution returned to this idea that we had stipulated that the accused was appointed to the subregion and because we stipulated to a fact about an appointment that nullifies the idea of a levee en masse. And, Your Honours, I don't know how many times we have to re-address arguments which we've already addressed, but it's -- the address is set out in our -- sorry, the response is set out in the response to the Prosecution motion to recall -- to call rebuttal evidence. You may recall that this same matter arose 31 January 2006, and it's paragraphs 28 to 29. "The Prosecution claims that it is a stipulated fact that Naser Oric was the commander of the subregion and that the Defence position has evolved away from this to Oric being relegated to a local commander. This entirely misrepresents the true position. The Defence denied all proposed stipulated facts to the effect that Naser Oric was a commander of either TO Srebrenica or TO Potocari. The Defence accepted only that Naser Oric was appointed the commander of the joint armed forces of the subregion Srebrenica in early November 1992. But then immediately denied the post stipulation following a link to it, namely that Naser Oric's command encompassed the geographical regions of several municipalities, namely Srebrenica, Bratunac, Vlasenica and Zvornik in Eastern Bosnia." In other words, the Defence accepted an appointment on paper only but denied that it ever took any effect as command encompassing any area whatsoever. And this was confirmed under the subregion existed only ever on paper by Dr. Mujkanovic and we had the slide there. "You told us the subregion never properly came into operation; would that be right. "That's right. "So is it right there wasn't ever any unified command for the enclaves of Kamenica, Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and Srebrenica? "As far as I know, no. There never was one." And later on he said: "It," the subregion concept, "didn't last long because very soon thereafter Konjevic Polje as did Cerska. So the whole concept lost practical significance. And it's a Prosecution witness and that was confirmed by numerous Defence witnesses. Now, Your Honours, the question of levee en masse is one of effective control. It's not question of whether someone was appointed on paper to a body which was never able to function. And I know Your Honours are going to decide whether there was a levee based on the facts, not on this stipulated fact and how it should be interpreted. In fact Your Honours, when Your Honours rendered your decision on rebuttal, I think you characterised our position as being the non-existence of the Muslim army and the corresponding appointment without substance of the accused as commander. I would put it slightly differently in that we -- we certainly acknowledge that there were groups fighting and fierce fighting in the region. We're not saying there was non-existence of any fighters, and I wouldn't say an appointment without substance. The notion is not that someone for no apparent reason decided to make an appointment. They were trying. They were certainly trying to create something as is only natural, but we just said that they didn't -- it didn't lead to anything. I move to the mens rea of command responsibility. Ms. Sellers said that our approach is not consistent with Tribunal jurisprudence in mentioning this malicious intent notion. But Akayesu is a decision of the Rwanda Tribunal, and there's a common Appeals Chamber. It's often said that the two Tribunals are identical twins linked at the head and the feet but not in the middle because they have a common Appeals Chamber and used to have a common Prosecutor. ICTR law is just as persuasive certainly as ICTY law. It may not be binding, but in fact the earlier decisions of this Tribunal were not binding either before the Aleksovski Appeals Chamber introduced the notion of precedence. But more fundamentally Ms. Sellers is trying to drive a wedge between customary international law and Tribunal law, and, yes, it's been said on I don't know on how many occasions the Tribunal must apply customary international law. Security Council had no power to create new law. And on this point it's actually set out bet in the Secretary-General's report on the ICTY Statute. And you have the reference there. "The International Tribunal should apply rules of international humanitarian law which are beyond any doubt part of customary law so that the problem of adherence of some but not all states to specific conventions does not arise." And in a decision in Delalic et al., 15 October 1996 of the Appeals Chamber or bench of the Appeals Chamber it said: "The Tribunal's Statute does not create new offences but rather serves to give the Tribunal jurisdiction over offences which are already part of customary law." So customary international law would always be relevant -- sorry, I realise I'm going too fast. I'll slow down. The commentary to the Additional Protocols will remain relevant the von Leeb case, high command case. All these sources are sources which can be applied by the Tribunal, and so there's no distinction -- fortunately no distinction between Tribunal law and customary international law. Ms. Sellers invoked policy arguments based on international humanitarian law, and this was in relation to aiding and abetting. You know, I don't know who formulated this alleged policy or where it's written or where we consult it, where we can consult it, and we can debate all day what would be a good policy but the policy is not law. Your Honours have to apply the law not some imagined policy. And states make law and they make customary international law, and you have to show state practice and opinio juris. You can't just skip over what is in fact a very -- what needs to be a very scholarly, careful exercise in looking at sources of law to just say, well, it's just good policy to extend the law to cover a new form of liability. It simply doesn't work that way. And when we talk about policy, we know what the attitude, let's say, of the US is to its troops not preventing pillage in Iraq. "Stuff happens," that's what Donald Rumsfeld said. We know that states don't hold themselves up to an angelic standard, although allegedly that would fit with the policy of the international humanitarian law. And, Your Honours, I say that there's no good policy to be served by a Balkanisation of the law, if I can put it that way, where we apply one law to Bosnia at this Tribunal but a law which we would never dream of applying to our own armies or our own countries, which Germany, the UK, the US, France, Italy, would never accept for their own commanders. So in my submission, that's a real danger that that will invent a policy version of the law for Bosnia which will -- which will only be applicable there and nowhere else. So if you hear the Prosecution invoke policy, I'd say reach for the statute book and the laws of armed conflict because it means that they know they don't have the law on their side. It's not good policy, no good policy is severed to be set by saying, well, if wrongs were done, we have to convict the accused of something. Our client is not a scapegoat for any wrongs done, and it's not as if a criminal trial is a failure if it results in a complete acquittal, although some seem to think so. Now, on aiding and abetting burning, the Prosecution's arguments have also now undergone a complete 180-degree shift. The Prosecution's theory in the indictment, in the pre-trial brief, and during the trial was that the accused, he personally encouraged burning by his presence, his presence, not presence of soldiers, his presence, in Fakovici, Bjelovac, Kravica and Jezestica on 7 January 1993. They didn't charge aiding and abetting for Ratkovici or for Jezestica in August 1992. But now, due to the invention of the Prosecution's L after the trial, we now find that our client is also being charged with responsibility for burning in Ratkovici and Jezestica on the basis of aiding and abetting, and much more fundamentally that he's now charged with his subordinates aiding and abetting civilians to commit burning. Now, that was never a part of their case. And in -- if it is permitted to be part of their case, then the goal-posts would have shifted 180 degrees, and we'd have to make submissions on a case we never had to deal with at trial At trial we had to deal with two issues for burning: Under 7(1), did our client aid and abet burning, and there was no evidence of that, and Dr. Mujkanovic on the contrary said that our client was fiercely opposed to burning; and then under 7(3) did our client subordinates, i.e., soldiers as they call it in their post-trial brief, under his effective control, did they burn? And there's been no evidence of that. So now in the week of closing arguments, despite the fact that even the Prosecution final brief only refers to soldiers burning, we're here discussing whether the accused could be held responsible for civilians burning. Now, I'll ask you to look at the closing brief. Paragraph 499, soldiers under the command of the accused unlawfully burnt houses. Paragraph 504, Ratkovici, soldiers under the command of the accused unlawfully burned houses. Paragraph 550, soldiers burned -- sorry, 570. Jezestica, paragraph 577, soldiers under the command of the accused unlawfully burned. Paragraph 614, soldiers burned. Paragraph 644 in the summary of conclusions soldiers burned. Paragraph 647, soldiers engaged in the systematic widespread and unlawful burning. We turn to Fakovici. Paragraph 652, soldiers under the command of the accused unlawfully burned houses. Paragraph 698, soldiers burned. Paragraph 738, soldiers burned. Then we turn to Bjelovac. Paragraph 742, units under the command and control of Naser Oric unlawfully destroyed Bosnian Serb property. And, again, paragraph 744, soldiers burned. Paragraph 852, soldiers burned. And then Kravica. Paragraph 858, units under the command and control of Naser Oric unlawfully destroyed Bosnian Serb property. Paragraph 860, still on Kravica, soldiers under the command of accused unlawfully burned houses and dwellings on a large scale during the course of the attack. Paragraph 902, soldiers burned. There's soldiers everywhere. Can anyone be in any doubt as to what the Prosecution's case was? I mean, only they seem to be in doubt as to what their case was. There's nothing on civilians burning there. And that was in the indictment too. Let's look at paragraph 27. In the course of such operations, Muslim armed units engaged in operations. In the course of such operations, Muslim armed units in the municipalities of Bratunac, Srebrenica and Skelani burnt and otherwise destroyed a minimum of 50 predominantly Serb villages and hamlets. And then we -- Muslim armed units, not civilians. We go to paragraph 37. Naser Oric -- no. Paragraph 37 stated Naser Oric from about June 1992 to August 1995 knew or had reason to know that his subordinates were about to commit such wanton destruction and plunder or had done so, et cetera, and failed to prevent or punish. So it's -- it's entirely obvious that their case, until we filed our final brief on the 17th of March, 2006, was that soldiers burned. But then we pointed out the fatal flaw in this reasoning that there were thousands of civilians in each action and that there was no evidence that a soldier from Skenderovici TO or from Potocari TO burnt a single house. And we said, and it's paragraph 4 of our response: "A remarkable feature of the Prosecution's presentation of the facts regarding wanton destruction is its total omission of any mention of the thousands of civilians," and it's tobari, "who went into every action. The Prosecution does not mention the existence of this phenomenon as they know that it is fatal to their case. Just how fatal it is may be demonstrated in a few sentences." And the next paragraph we demonstrated, we say convincingly, why that argument was untenable. So the Prosecution then says, okay, well, then let's say that civilians burned and the soldiers aided and abetted. Even that's not in the indictment. It's not in the pre-trial brief or the final brief. Civilians burned and fighters aided and abetted. Well, maybe fighters also burned. Or maybe fighters and civilians. We don't know, we don't care. Whatever happened, just convict the accused for it. That's essentially what they're saying. Now, if that's what passes for proving your case beyond a reasonable doubt, international criminal law is in dire straits. It's in danger of losing all credibility. Your Honours are well aware of the fundamental right of the accused to know what the Prosecution's case is from the start of the trial and not to learn what their case is weeks after the last witness testified So that's all I want to say about aiding and abetting, burning. I won't even address the arguments on the merits about whether fighters aided and abetted civilians by their presence. It's not a case we had notice of. It's not a case we're called on to answer, and there is in any event no evidence of it. On wanton destruction, I'll just make three points. Ms. Sellers said that we've conflated military necessity a necessity. Well, I don't think we have, and if Your Honours are in any confusion as to the analysis in our closing speech, then I'm happy, more than happy to answer any questions on that. We set out precisely what the approach should be and we haven't conflated or confused anything. Ms. Sellers seems to wish to put the burden of proof on us regarding military necessity, but the law is absolutely clear the burden is on the Prosecution to show that any destruction was not justified by military necessity. That's their burden, not on us to prove that any damage was justified militarily. And now thirdly, I just say you get a sense of the Prosecution's unrealistic approach to international humanitarian law when you see this. Ms. Sellers said on Friday: "Now, it's possible that the rocket launcher in a town is a legitimate military object." You'll note that it's only possible, only possibly okay to go and disable the enemy's rocket launcher. So there's even a possibility you might have to write the Serbs a cheque for their rocket launcher after you've destroyed it or stolen it. Even though it's shooting at you and killing you. It's still not clear in international humanitarian law whether you have a right to go and get that rocket launcher. Now, you can see if that's their approach, you can see why they think any damage must be wanton. But the Prosecution's approach would outlaw pretty much all warfare. I mean, you couldn't use heavy artillery because you might hit something other than a legitimate military object; you couldn't drop bombs from the air. They would all be outlawed because you might hit something other than something which is purely a military objective. And this is what I mean about the danger that IHR will lose all credibility because of this armchair theorising which has absolutely no bearing on military reality. And if you speak to military lawyers, they'll certainly tell you, and people have to fight wars, that international humanitarian law is a lot more realistic about what happens in war than the Prosecution. And

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS SAID
utterances.text: "The Defence notion is much more generalised that towns and areas and villages offers a definite military advantage." Well, first that is the approach endorsed by international humanitarian law, and we addressed this in paragraph 35 of our closing brief. According to the UK Manual on the Law on Armed Conflict: "An area of land can, thus be a military objective, areas of land such as hills, defiles and bridgeheads" can be military objectives. And under military necessity it even says this: Private homes and churches even may be destroyed if necessary for military operations." Those the hostages case. And in my submission, Your Honours, it's obvious that if a civilian object is used for a military purpose, it loses its civilian status. If a school becomes a barracks and there are soldiers in there with their weapons, obviously the school is a legitimate military object. If trenches go through someone's house, that house becomes a legitimate military objective. If a hill has an artillery piece, then capturing that hill and destroying the artillery piece and maybe even destroying the house which it's hiding behind might be a legitimate military objective. One has to be pragmatic and realistic about what's essentially war and people fighting for their lives. And in the history of warfare, it's obvious armies take whole areas, towns, villages, hills, beachheads because they offer military objective. They don't tiptoe around the enemy. You can't imagine the Normandy landing and the troops arriving and tiptoeing around the Germans and making sure that they didn't displace a flower pot or something which wasn't a legitimate military objective. That's not warfare. Warfare is quite other. So if our approach seems generalised, it's for at least three reasons: First, international humanitarian law justifies it; second, the Prosecution's approach has been generalised, talking about areas being damaged without any detailed inventory of what was destroyed, when it was destroyed, how it was destroyed, why it was destroyed and by whom. And so as I say, and as we said in our 65 ter conference, for us to have to be specific when the Prosecution was general is deeply unfair. If the Prosecution just say, well, generally things are destroyed. Now you, Defence, you go in and do a detailed inventory of what was a legitimate military objective. That's not fair. The break is normally at 10.45 is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly I'll break at this point, if it's convenient. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a 30-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Now, before the break, we were dealing with this question of a generalised approach to the question of wanton destruction, and I mentioned a couple of reasons why our approach might seem generalised, namely that international humanitarian law so provides, and also that the Prosecution's approach has not been a specific one. But more importantly, perhaps, the Serbs' approach was generalised, if one can put it that way. They billeted soldiers in houses in the villages surrounding Srebrenica. They kept their weapons and grenades in houses, in barns, in schools, and in warehouses. They put heavy artillery in the centre of villages, and then they counter-attacked with heavy artillery, they did so indiscriminately, and that's all a matter of evidence. Now, what in fact happened in early 1992 is that many of these Serb villages evacuated the civilian population or a substantial part of it, and we saw that, for example, in P448 in which Jovan Nikolic stated: "And the people of this village," and he's referring to Kravica, "being aware of the beasts that surrounded us relocated their weak to Serbia, and we stayed to defend the village the best we could." And you'll find similar evidence for Bjelovac and Fakovici and some of the other locations. Now, the Serbs used a sledgehammer to crack a nut, if one can put it that way, and the Prosecution in their presentation of the case has used a sledgehammer to crack a nut. Yet we are expected, it seems, to use tweezers to sift through the ruins and to show who did what and why it was done, and in my submission that's not the correct approach. Now, to get a sense of the approach, the tactics of the Serbs in relation to Srebrenica, in relation to these villages that we've looked at, I would ask you to look at D928, and we see there -- and this is an order of the Serbs: "Consolidate the Fakovici battalion as soon as possible and give it the task to penetrate as deep as possible into the area of Srebrenica using the territory of Serbian villages and attack Srebrenica." And that's from the command post in Bratunac. I'll ask you to pay careful attention to those words "using the territory of Serbian villages to launch attacks on Srebrenica." That was the tactic of the Bosnian Serb army, to attack Srebrenica from these very areas surrounding Srebrenica. And so that will give you a sense of the military necessity involved in the actions which we've seen in the indictment. They used the whole territory to attack. They evacuated women and children, and they made the surrounding villages essentially militarised areas. And during attacks, you've seen during each and every attack the Serbs were shoot from the houses on the attackers. And we have proof of that in, as I say, every action, and we can review just a sample of that evidence, firstly with Ratkovici. This is the evidence of Omer Ramic. First of all, he said: "We found a mortar in a barn. The other one, another one was in a village." So again when you hear of banks burning, don't assume that that must have been wanton destruction. There were weapons kept in barns. And we go to the next slide. "We could see anti-aircraft gun which was next to the school at Pantici," and this is a hamlet of Ratkovici, "and there were machine-guns from houses. You could see how they were mounting onto houses and there was a yellow gun with these PAM and PAT guns, and that's anti-aircraft machine-guns and anti-aircraft guns. And they were being used in order to shoot at people who were looking for food. And dozens of people were killed and wounded on that day." So, again, shooting from houses, the very houses which were allegedly damaged or destroyed. And then we can see for the next slide. "I said that I got to Gornji Ratkovici and the Serb army was firing from the houses, so there was a fight and then the Serb forces withdrew." Yet again, shooting from those houses, those houses thereby becoming legitimate military objectives. We'll see the same when we turn to Jezestica that the front lines went straight through Jezestica and right by the houses. That was the evidence of Sidik Ademovic. And we were referring or quoting there from a Defence exhibit, D35, in which it's the staff, the Serb Crisis Staff determining defence lines in all those settlements which were all in the Kravica local commune. And you see that the Defence lines went through Jezestica, Jaglici, Djermani, and Veresinje. And Sidik Ademovic was asked about that, and he said: "All those lines were known to me, but what I had direct connection with was Siljkovici," which again is mentioned in the indictment. And then he indicated the areas, showing his knowledge of the area: "And to be brief, does this document reliably describe the front line on the ground? "Answer: Yes." And if we turn to Fakovici, Nesib Buric testified, and this is relating to the action on the 5th of October, 1992. "And in between the houses, there were mortars of 82- and 60-millimetre calibre. And if I may add, there were ramparts and bunkers and dugouts that were made of sandbags and crates, ammunition crates that were filled with earth. The greatest problem that we had was the place that we called salas. It's place where we keep wheat. And they dug out a trench next to it and put some concrete in as well. And they kept firing from there in all direction around Fakovici." And then later he clarified that it's not just one barn which is a regular feature with the outhouses. "But each house had its own and fire was opened from behind each one of the houses." So that's the evidence, that from each one of the houses the Serbs were shooting. And as I say, the houses beyond any doubt may therefore be fired upon. And we can see the next slide as well. About the numbers of soldiers in Fakovici on that day. "Question: You referred to several hundreds of Serb soldiers. What's your best estimate for how many Serb soldiers why fighting in Fakovici on the 5th of October, 1992? "Answer: If we have the information that in Fakovici there was a military battalion between 3 and 600 soldiers." Obviously that's between 300 and 600 soldiers. And again we've been if Fakovici. We've seen it's a small area, and if in that small area you have between 300 and 600 soldiers shooting from houses, one can imagine there will quite naturally be a certain amount of damage to those houses, not to mention the damage caused by the Serb counter-attack with heavy artillery. We'll see the next slide, Bjelovac. Azir Malagic testified -- and again about the action in December 1992: "And then they pulled back into the outlying houses in Jovanovici which were like real bunkers. They had placed sandbags around the houses and turned them into machine-gun nests. And then they really started firing at our fighters who were trying to get into those trenches." Yet again, houses a part of the action, a part of what the Serbs were using for a military purpose. And not just one house but every one of the houses. And in the next slide he went on. "After the Serb forces withdrew to the houses, they opened fierce fire at our fighters above Jovanovici, and fierce fighting ensued for about half an hour. ... But what surprised us was that they first shelled the houses. They were probably confused." i.e., the Serbs selling their own houses. "And did you also lose your PAM at those houses? "Yes. The PAM had to fire at those houses.
