We used that the most because tremendous reinforcements were coming from the direction of Bjelovac towards Jovanovici, so the PAM was firing at those people and at the houses from which fire was being directed at our fighters." And he goes on to say: "A transporter would be firing from Bjelovac from a PAM, they would be firing at the houses, they would be firing at us, so we would have to find better shelter so that we would not be exposed to that fire." And we can now look at the next slide. And this is for Kravica and Jezestica and the 7th of January, 1993. And this is D005. And he said that he knew that there were weapons, Serb weapons in the houses in Kravica and that they were fired from. "As far as the houses in Obackici are concerned," and that's in the local commune of Kravica, "that you were able to see in the course of 1992, were they merely used as residential dwellings for civilians or were they used for some other purposes? "They were used only for military purposes because the civilians headed towards Serbia at the very start of the war." And that's confirmation of the document we saw that the Serbs did in fact evacuate civilians at the start of the war. "When you say that they were used for military purposes, can you specify what this was about? "One could see" -- and this is referring to the actual day of the 7th of January. "One could see soldiers entering and exiting the houses. One could see them opening fire next to the houses. I saw a mortar there." And this was confirmed also, if we can see the next slide, where he went on further to add: "From your testimony so far, did I understand probably that not only trenches were used to open fire at Muslim villages? "They didn't have much use of trenches. They felt strong and they thought they would be able to deal with the entire situation from their houses rather than from trenches." And if we'd see the next slide. We have even in Serb documents D938, it's a book, I believe. We see it written there and again describing the action on the 7th of January: "I went to five soldiers to the house of an inhabitant Vaso, and we fired at them from there." Now, Your Honours, this case about wanton destruction is concerned is about damage to houses, and it's surely highly significant that in every one of these actions the Serbs were in fact shooting from those houses and that there was very heavy gun fights on each occasion. And finally we can see Ibro Alic as well testifying on this matter. "Was the shooting coming from the houses or from some other location behind the houses. "The shooting came mostly from where I was, from those houses, and higher up, where other people were. I think there was four-barrelled weapon, and I was told that it was being used all the time incessantly and there was shooting coming from those houses all the time. Basically, there was shooting coming oust every single house." So, Your Honours, I think I need add nothing more to the testimony there which speaks eloquently for itself. Where soldiers shoot from houses those houses become military objectives. Now, Your Honour, I move to a new -- a new theme, entirely new, and it's responding to Mr. di Fazio's remarks about Professor Bilic and his evidence and how you evaluate it. And I don't have much to respond to to his arguments which he made on Friday. I just make four points. First, the Prosecution seek to suggest that the fact that there are only forensics on the Fejzic and Salihovic signatures on their exhibits is somehow the Defence's fault. Well, the fact is they're their exhibits and why didn't they simply do what we did? Fejzic is alive. Why didn't they contact Fejzic and simply do what we did, ask for some sample signatures, look at his official documents. There's no reason on earth why they shouldn't do that. Salihovic, again, why didn't they do simply what we did, a bit of investigative work to get copies of documents from the archives and to have forensic analysis done on those signatures. It's not our fault that they didn't do that. And in fact we know that the Prosecution has a certified signature of Salihovic provided by the Serbs. And just for the record, the ERN is 03720854 to 03720855. In our submission, that signature looks different from the ones on exhibits, and it wasn't disclosed to us under Rule 68. That's another matter, but I simply mention that in this connection. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You say certified signature of Salihovic. Certified by whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: By the Serb authorities. It's -- essentially it's a document from the OBS, and it says -- there's a short document with a signature purporting to be Hamid Salihovic, and then attached with it is a note saying signature of Hamid Salihovic, commander for security and intelligence of Srebrenica armed forces. And that's a document which we found. So why didn't they ask their --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not in the record however, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, it was on EDS, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. We don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, I just mention that. Now, Mr. di Fazio gave an example of what if a ballistics expert were to testify that a bullet had been fired from a weapon and yet the bullet was not -- well, I would only make one point on that which is that you'll recall Dr. Stankovic's report referring to a piece of paper allegedly with the name Kostadin Popovic on it, and I would simply say what's sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander, and if their argument is correct then surely Dr. Stankovic's report is of utterly no probative value because we did not see that piece of paper and that's one of the items referred to in his report. And finally, I've made the point before, but if the Prosecution really thought it would assist Your Honours to have those non-contentious documents they shouldn't be objected to us -- or, rather, Mr. di Fazio shouldn't have stood up and made point of objecting to them being tendered; rather, they should have invited them to be tendered right from the start. Now, sentencing. I just have to correct one or two matters stated by Mr. di Fazio on Friday about sentencing. Now, first in terms of the statements of Mr. Tedder and Mr. Kelly, you know, they can say what they like about whether it was minor cooperation or major cooperation. My point is that they shouldn't pretend that that doesn't exist at all. They shouldn't state untruths to the Trial Chamber such as the accused never agreed any evidence when he did. You know, they're not entitled to ignore the facts. And that's unlawyerly. We were accused of being unlawyerly. That's unlawyerly, to make categorical statements which cannot be backed up by the facts. Now, Mr. di Fazio said this on Friday in he relation to remorse: There have been no expressions of remorse that you have heard in the Trial Record nor in any of the sentencing submissions made by the Defence on behalf of the accused." And then he said: "There has been none in anything that I've heard in the time that I've been involved in this case." Now, Your Honours, the Prosecution made exactly the same point in their final brief and we responded to that exact point to say this: And it's paragraph 155: "The Prosecution says that the accused has shown no sign of guilt or remorse. This is only natural in a trial on a not guilty plea." Paragraph 156: "The Defence has, however, consistently shown consideration and empathy for the suffering of victims during the trial." And I refer to my words in the Rule 98 bis submissions when I said this: "It's clear that people were badly beaten in Srebrenica in the prison. We don't deny that, and we say it's tragic and terribly wrong that it ever happened, and we have every sympathy for those who suffered and for the families of those who died. But we only say that those crimes are not attributable in any way to Naser Oric." Now those remarks which we made are the remarks of our client made on his behalf. Those are part of our submissions, if you like, on sentencing. And when I heard Mr. di Fazio make those remarks about there being no sign of essentially any compassion throughout the trial, I felt sure he didn't even carefully read our closing brief, otherwise he would not have said that. And it's that lawyerly and is that professional? And is what the Prosecution filed as a final brief on the 17th of March, 1993, which I invite the public to obtain copies, is that professional? And I ask the Prosecution to be careful about accusing us of being unlawyerly in light of their own conduct. The Defence showed compassion for every witness who testified about beatings, and you can see on the next three slides. When C007 testified. I said to him: "Good morning, Witness. Now just so you know, and perhaps to put you at your ease, we're not to challenge that you received terrible treatment and suffered horribly in 1992 and early 1993, and that you still suffer seriously from that. We just say that it has nothing to do with our client, Naser Oric. Just so that's clear firstly." And then when Mr. Nikolic testified I said: "Now, I'm going to ask you a few questions about the beatings that you suffered, and I want to make very clear, before I asked you these questions, that we don't wish, of course, to minimise in any way what you suffered, but just to be clear about what your injuries were. So I hope that's clear." And then Mr. Ivanovic when he testified. "Question: Now, I want to make it very clear that we don't challenge that you were beaten in Srebrenica and that it was a horrible experience; I want that to be a hundred per cent clear. What we do say is that Naser Oric was not in the reception room in the prison. That's what my questions are concerned with. Do you understand that?" His answer was: "I fully understand what you mean." I think he not only understood but I think he appreciated that remark. Now, as Your Honour pointed out in a criminal trial where the accused maintains his innocence, it's not just difficult it's impossible for him -- and nonsensical for him to say at the same time I'm sorry for what I did, since our case is that he did not do it. The most he can do, the only thing he can do is express sympathy in the way that we have done and as you've seen in those slides. So the Prosecution is deaf to those words. And Mr. di Fazio talked about the impact of the crimes and he said: "Those communities were in the main destroyed forever and the people have not gone back to those villages and resumed their lives." Now, it's a pity that Mr. di Fazio was not on the on-site visit with us as he would have seen that Kravica, Fakovici, and Bjelovac certainly are very much there with their communities, their Serb communities. I don't believe many Muslims have returned to Bjelovac. But it suits the Prosecution to say that those villages have been completely destroyed forever, so they say it even though it's untrue. And I don't know how time and again throughout the 16 months of this trial the Prosecution can make statements which are not founded in any fact. In my submission, that's how the case came to be, statements made without facts to back them up. And the Prosecution's sentencing recommendation should be founded on fact, not fiction, and that was our point. And so, Your Honours, I would conclude simply by saying that the only appropriate sentence is in fact no sentence as justice in this case requires nothing less than a full acquittal of all charges. Our client will in fact take up your offer of a -- the opportunity to say a few words but that would conclude my rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, we'll invite your client to address us after we have put questions to both of you. In other words, he'll have the final -- Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, only after you put the questions the Prosecution would like to very briefly address the Trial Chamber prior to Mr. Oric speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to that, because I don't see what would justify further submissions by the Prosecution. They had two days of closing argument. We had two days of closing argument. They had rebuttal on Friday. We had rejoinder Friday and today. If Your Honours have questions for the Prosecution, of course they can answer that. But I would vigorously oppose the notion that the Prosecution can have another round of submissions. They've had enough time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. There are not going to be any further submissions. But if I am reading the Prosecution well, they -- I understand that following our invitation to your client to address us, I understand that they may wish to make a submission on that and only that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. If I may then reserve the right to respond to their response to our rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do I read you well Ms. Sellers or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was precisely what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I would have imagined so. And if anything, I can even anticipate what the submission is. That there is a Rule which specifies exactly when an accused can address but that doesn't exclude other opportunities. Yes. Now, we have some questions for you. Judge Brydensholt doesn't have any questions. I don't have any questions either. I did have before, but I think more or less I have had you address them sufficiently. Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I have some questions. The first one is addressed to both parties. Perhaps either of you may answer it. I would like to come back to the role of the War Presidency. If we compared the War Presidency to a normal situation where you had a magistrate of a city consisting of a mayor and some other people around him and some sort of a city parliament, now, what functions would the War Presidency have? Both of -- both functions of being the chief executive authority in a place and/or also of making certain general decisions in terms of giving norms, setting norms, setting guidelines and so on? That's my first question. There may be additional ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll respond first. In terms of the War Presidency as has been put forward in this case, it appears that under the former Yugoslavia there were situations when the municipal executive authority would move to war mode, if we can say that. Also, as the evidence has shown, as presented by the Office of the Prosecutor but also Defence evidence, is that we're dealing with a situation where the de jure powers of the War Presidency might not be in a straight line that they would have been in had communications been received from Sarajevo and Srebrenica as it pertained to War Presidency. So there's been some discussion as to whether they were legally set up or not. The Prosecution wants to move more to how do they function in the manner in which they were set up. We had this discussion about what's written on paper and what happened in fact. And our position, Your Honour, is that the paper that was emitted, whether it be from the War Presidency or military authorities, was not completely disconnected with what happened on the ground. As a matter of fact, there was probably more a reflection in the paperwork as to what happened on the ground than a non-reflection, particularly given that paper was such a vital resource. The Prosecution would state that the War Presidency in this case was a Presidency that was not a military hierarchy. If they were the Supreme Command governing command from the civilian and even if there were the military functioning of Naser Oric and other military units within Srebrenica, Hajrudin Avdic did not give orders to the military. If the Trial Chamber thinks that because they were the supreme power of government, then that merely places Naser Oric back in the chain of command. It doesn't obviate his responsibility. It might implicate the responsibility of Hajrudin Avdic. The Prosecution's position is that doesn't in any way diminish his liability or guilt. But from how the facts have emerged it seems to me that the War Presidency dealt with many of the civilian functions within the town. Becir Bogilovic was quite certain. He was civilian police. They dealt with civilian functions, in terms of dividing up food that might have come back after the attacks, in terms of taking care of refugees being housed in certain buildings, in terms of having the refugee population be able to be contained enough so that the city could continue to function, and then it seems that they had quite a -- quite a role in holding meetings and discussing problems within the town, but we have no evidence that's presented and the Prosecution would submit that they did not orders to the military police, to the military in general, and that they were often, as P84 shows, were a bit taken aback when they were not included in just generalised discussions about attacks or discussions about important things that the military would undertake. I hope I've answered Judge Eser's question. If not, please redirect me to certain specific parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, do you wish to address the Chamber on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I would will refer to the evidence of Mustafa Sacirovic who said: "The War Presidency was the supreme organ of Srebrenica municipality." I would refer you also to the evidence of Witness Brkic and Hogic to the same effect; and also to D282; and D283 on that subject. And my learned friend just referred to P84. If you turn to page 5050, 02115050 there is a discussion of the War Presidency and Ramiz: "The War Presidency substitutes for the Assembly. The members of the War Presidency are the Municipal Assembly President," et cetera. And then further down, hierarchy. "It discusses and assesses the war situation and takes decisions." He's referring to the War Presidency. "It is both the supreme authority and the Supreme Command." And so our submission is that the War Presidency was the supreme authority on the ground. I can't answer Your Honour's question about what it would be in a normal situation because there isn't evidence of that. I don't want to give evidence myself, and above all else, obviously Srebrenica was not a normal situation. The situation in 1992, 1993 is that it was the supreme authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, I have a follow-up question. If it is -- if we assume that the War Presidency had been supreme authority in the city and they had to deal with quite a lot of issues which in a normal situation would be distributed between different authorities, bodies, and so on, and if we also assume that a supreme authority in a city would delegate certain functions to lower bodies or groups or persons, and if we also take into account the special situation in Srebrenica because there has been a lot -- as it has been described in various ways a lot of chaos, is it possible to think of a clear-cut separation of the various powers, possibilities taken within a place, or would it be normal that there is a transgressing of certain areas from one to the other or, to put it this way, if we assume that with all the higher levels of War Presidencies there have been other bodies to deal with certain issues, and if it was a rather difficult situation, is it thinkable, at least, that at certain times the duties or powers of two different bodies have been confused?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, a couple of points come to mind. Firstly, we don't want to enter into the realm of speculation about what might have happened or could have happened. We have the trial record. We have the evidence of witnesses and that's obviously what we're basing ourselves on. That would be my first point. Secondly, you mentioned cities and an authority with many powers. Well, at the same time, this isn't the Greater London Council. It's not the City of New York. We've heard evidence on a very micro -- sort of microlevel of Avdic interacting with Jusufovic and others. And if we're talking, as I assume we are, about detention and trying to work out who was in charge of what, we don't have to speculate about what might have happened with different lines being crossed. We have the evidence there. We have the president of the War Presidency dealing with the chief of the civilian police, receiving reports from Mirzet Halilovic, receiving reports from Becir Bogilovic. We have the evidence of Mustafa Sacirovic, Djilovic. And, yes, there were lots of people in Srebrenica, tens of thousands of people, but when you come to something like who was dealing with what, we've had very concrete evidence in this case of what the War Presidency was doing and what the members of the War Presidency were involved in. And so, in my submission, there's no need to speculate about what might have happened and how things could have been confused. But, thirdly, having said that, of course there is evidence that things were highly confused in Srebrenica, and certainly we've made a point that it was anarchy and it was chaos. But one couldn't go from that -- I don't know if this is the thrust of Your Honour's question, but to say, oh, well, if there was confusion, then possibly the War Presidency was not responsible for detention, possibly the military was. Speculations of that nature, if that's where Your Honour is heading, are utterly fruitless. We have evidence and the evidence -- clearly shows the War Presidency being responsible for detention as I've set out today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, you see --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Judge Eser, I don't know whether you wanted me to address that or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: My questions are addressed to both parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. If I just might then follow my learned friend in that. Is -- Defence counsel talks about specific information as compared with possibilities. The Prosecution will try and say quite briefly, because Your Honours are quite aware, that it's June 15th that we have the creation of the military police created by the Srebrenica TO, July 1st that we have documents that show decisions made by the Crisis Staff, it included creation of the War Presidency, and again the affirmation the military police and the communications system, Hamed Alic communication system being set up that would serve both -- and this is the issue that I think Your Honour is reaching, that would serve both the military police and the War Presidency, had a civilian/military role and even a role that took it back to Bratunac. That civilian authorities, the military authorities at times met together, yes. That there might have been a type of sharing of powers or sharing of resolutions of problems, yes. But let's not confuse what was specific information about one incident and generalise it to information, such as Mirzet Halilovic being a -- subordinated to Becir Bogilovic. Why subordinate -- why resubordinate someone to someone who is already subordinated? So there were certain lines that were clearer than one would believe, and then confusion might have ensued afterwards, after October 14. But Your Honours, I think that both the Defence and the Prosecution can state that the situation in Srebrenica at times followed what would have been by the book under Yugoslav law, and at times it reacted to the situation that was -- that it found itself in on the ground, both the civilian authorities and the military authorities. That, in a way, diminishes our case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Before I put my next question I would like to make sure that I am not asking for speculations. My question -- my next question is relating to the law, and here we had evidence or submissions with regard to the military police, submissions which would say there was no legal basis for establishing a military police at all. There has been no clearer description of the duties and authorities they would have. Now, what would be the legal conclusion? What legal conclusion would have to be drawn? My question goes again to both parties. There would be two main solutions if we assume that there was no legal basis for establishing a military police, but nevertheless, there have been certain people within the SUP and the building behind the building. Now, if these people in the building lacked authority, now, what -- there could be two solutions. One solution could be since there was no authority, there was no duty to protect. That would mean that you -- a non-authorised person could take prisoners, put them at a certain place and leave them without any protection. That would be one legal conclusion. Now, the alternative conclusion could be that even if somebody has no authority to do a certain thing, to take a certain decision, to perform a certain action, but if he does it, he has a certain duty with regard to the persons concerned. So even that means if he takes this position, even if there was no authority from a legal point of view, at least by taking prisoners there was developed or there was resulted some duty to take care of those people in order to let them unprotected. Now, my question to both parties is: What legal opinion would you have to this issue, to this alternative? What are the results? What conclusion can be drawn from the lack of authority with regard to having, nevertheless, some sort of duty to protect peoples who are under -- under the protection or under the possibility to deal with? Now, you could also ask when you are a guard, even if I have not been authorised to be a guard, when you are a guard you become a guardian with regard to protecting the people concerned. That would be the question I have to the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers. If you want to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. Your Honour, the Prosecution's position is that as we described earlier there might be a bit of -- of a -- of a breach between the de jure authority coming from Sarajevo and Tuzla. I mean, just put those arguments to side because we're going to now what in essence the military police whether it was up de facto, just meaning outside of the realm of the Tuzla and Sarajevo establishment. It was established according to what the situation in Srebrenica and those who declared themselves to be the authorities, first the military authorities until the civilian authorities were set up. So there was a de facto type of legality of the military police, and therefore we could say the guards at the detention centre in both the first and the second segment. Now, for that individual guard, yes, you decide to be a guard, you do have a duty, a responsibility. That would take place if we just had a guard in any situation in a prison whether we were at war or not. Here we have guards that are part of a military structure, the military structure that evolved in Srebrenica. Now, to show that the military structure, and in particular the military police, considered that there were duties and their obligations is that we have a lot of documentation, documentary evidence that talks about when people steal weapons, when people steal food, to be arrested, to be brought to a prison. Yes. There was not this unrealistic sense of responsibility. Not only in terms of the civilian population but in terms of the military population among themselves. And, Judge Eser, I don't think that it is a leap to say that the guards who were at the detention centres, irrespective of how the military police were structured in terms of law with Sarajevo and Tuzla did have duties to the prisoners. In addition, international humanitarian law is applicable to that situation. We know that the international community expects that when you're in the hands of the enemy or when you're outside of combat and placed in detention situations that the military guarding you, or the powers that are guarding you, do have duties and those duties entail the non-commission of crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Sellers. Ultimately at the end of the day the bottom line is would Naser Oric be responsible for it. This is the whole question that needs it be addressed. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, precisely Your Honour. I would make just really two broad points. And one is, to a certain extent, an objection to this -- this way of proceeding, because, Your Honours, if we were on appeal before a court appeal could discuss different theories of the law and think of different scenarios. I emphasised before the Prosecution brings this case, they have to give us notice of any theories which they intend to use, and that, Your Honour Judge Eser, if at this stage you suggest or devise new theories that a duty to act might arise from an omission. Well, I simply make this point, Your Honour, that it's too late for any new theories. They have to be set out by the Prosecution. And I want to make that point, that it's not just -- we're not just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're disputing theories, Mr. Jones. Let's calm down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honours, in terms of the evidence, the War Presidency set up the military police. The War Presidency is responsible for their acts. The civilian police were authorised and duty-bound to protect the detainees because the civilian police were holding the detainees, as I've outlined today. And so if the Prosecution wants to argue that there was a duty to act and an omission to act, that's something which should have been in the indictment. It should have been in their pre-trial brief. And then that's why I'm reluctant to -- to even get into the whole theoretical aspect of this debate, because I see -- I think -- correct me if I've misunderstood you, Judge Eser, but the essence of your question is if the military police was not actually authorised, not properly set up de jure, and we've argued that the Territorial Defence could not have a military police component based on various documents, there were, if de facto, nonetheless something calling itself the military police itself set up, and if it detains people -- and as I say, the evidence doesn't support any of these propositions, but I'm going with your scenario, that the military police therefore detained people, wouldn't that create a duty to act and, therefore, a omission to protect those people a corresponding legal responsibility? That's how I understand your question, and I think that's what you're driving at. And my response only is factually that's not -- that's not the scenario, and that, secondly, these omissions and duties to act are not pled in the indictment, and it's not something which we are called upon to respond to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I really would make clear, Mr. Jones, that I -- that you brought a lot of legal arguments here, and if the Judges want to have clarification with regard to certain legal arguments, further information, I think it's completely appropriate to ask, completely proper to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And so just to refer to your own or the Defence's presentation with regard to the question of committing, you referred to the Krstic case, and you even brought it here, that committing covers physically perpetrating a crime or engendering a culpable omission in relation of criminal law. I think it's a very important question to ask whether there was an omission or not, because an omission is considered as a form of committing. Now, since you referred to the German law at various places and since you showed that you are familiar with the German law, I would like to ask you what the position is with regard to the following: As you certainly know, there are in many -- not only the German law, in many domestic laws there's a duty to act which may be by virtue of taking a factual position. In Germany it's called "garantenstellung kraft ubernahme." There is another duty to act which may result from antecedent conduct that refers, in particular, to the case where some -- where a person has been brought in the situation in which this person is not -- unable to take care of himself or herself. Then those who have brought this person into this situation have a certain duty to protect. Now, there is a clear link, I think, between your own reference to committing by acts or omissions -- and you may remember that in our 98 bis decision we also made clear that both acts and omissions may incur responsibility. That's an important question which has to be clarified: On what kind of duty it may be based that an endangered person should be protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. No, Your Honour, I -- when I cited Krstic, I was well aware that it referred to the omission, and I imagined that Your Honour Judge Eser would raise that part of the definition. And this is why I go back to the point, that this isn't merely a question of what are possible legal theories. It's a question of what did the Prosecution allege. Now, if you look at Krstic, it's engendering a culpable omission. Now, the Prosecution hasn't alleged what culpable omission was committed by Naser Oric's subordinates. They would have to allege that in the indictment. They would have to say Naser Oric is responsible because his subordinates engendered a culpable omission, and they have to describe what culpable omission consisted of clearly so we know the case we have to meet, and then they have to prove it as well. And I referred last week to the complete evidential void as to how people got into the prison. There are mens rea requirements. A culpable omission is not any omission. It's not negligent omission. It's a culpable omission. And especially if you're talking about something like murder. Then it's not merely, as I say, leaving the door open which makes you a murderer. And I gave an example in our closing brief that if a husband walks out the front door and leaves the door open, maybe he shouldn't have done, maybe that was negligent, and he omitted to close the door and a murderer goes in and kills his wife, is he a murderer? Of course not. It's not any omission. It's a culpable omission. So my point is that has to be pleaded, firstly; and then, secondly, it has to be proved. And I mentioned today how Radic and Ivanovic spoke of how they were only beating in the evenings. Now, did the guards culpably omit to lock the doors, or did they lock the doors and the doors got broken down, as they said, people breaking in to mistreat the prisoners? Did the guards -- did the guards notice the detainees were being mistreated? We've got no evidence of that. We've got no evidence that the guards said, "Oh, look, you're in a bad way." I'm sure the Prosecution would like at the eleventh hour to say, "Oh, well, that can be inferred," but these are all matters which have to be pleaded and which have to be proved. And that's why, as I say, at the eleventh hour saying, "Well, maybe we can put our case on this theory, on a theory of omissions," is far too late for that, even as a matter of law one can imagine a case which might be built on that. And I would add, Your Honour, and I also made this point very clear in our closing brief, what -- what normally happens in this sort of a case, the case Your Honour has in mind where you have a camp and you have detainees who are there and they are being mistreated -- and it's quite reasonable, and I accept that if you have a camp with barbed wire around it and you have a camp commander, if people get in and mistreat the detainees, then he's going to be responsible, because after all, it's not very savory to say, "Well, that's all right. People got in and mistreated these detainees and no one's responsible." No. But that's -- that's your camp commander JCE case. That's why the third type of JCE evolved, to say if the whole detention itself is criminal, then -- you know, then of course you can hold the commander responsible for everything that happens. This is a case not based on JCE. It's based on classic 7(3) superior to subordinate liability, and the Prosecution has to allege and prove every single element of the mens rea and actus reus. That would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you. And in addition, if I may add, there is always, at the end of it, that any law that applies to this case must first and foremost be proven to have been part of international law or customary law at the time of the commission of the crimes if these crimes were committed. So next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Of course, I only took up what you call theories, but I think they are part of the law. But particularly with regard to the law, I was a little bit irritated -- or not "irritated" is not the right word. I was puzzled a little bit when with regard to the interpretation of Article 7(3) you would say it is up to the Prosecution to show that the interpretation of the Defence is absurd. Now, is it your position that the burden of proof does not only refer to evidence and facts as is all over the world, or that also the burden of proof is also with regard to the interpretation of the law?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour has to take what I said there in context. And I don't want to spend another hour on my submissions on committing, but you'll recall the argument was -- was not that. The argument is this: Article 7(3) says committing. It doesn't refer to any other forms of liability. Now, Article 7(1) also refers to committing, and it distinguishes it from aiding and abetting. So we say that obviously committing doesn't included aiding and abetting, because in 7(1) the two terms are contrasted. That's a classic argument -- forgive me. The term escapes me. But it's clear from the plain words of Article 7(3) that it's committing. That's -- that's the very first point of view that in a word -- the same word in the same Article is going to have the same meaning. Then I said it's a matter of statutory interpretation that you first of all read the plain words of an Article, and only if that leads to absurdity or repugnance do you have to look for another meaning. Now, it's the Prosecution who is saying, "We don't like "committing" just meaning committing. We want it to include something else." So of course because they're challenging the plain interpretation they have the burden. And I'm not talking about burden in a broader sense of a criminal trial. They're the ones who are challenging a plain reading of an Article, so of course they have to show that that interpretation leads to absurdity or repugnance. It's clear principle, a statutory interpretation set out in Celebici and in other places. And then I said, secondly, a literal interpretation is also a principle of statutory interpretation and "committing" means "committing." It means physically committing in any -- in any basic sense of the English word. Then I said, on top of that, and again it's a matter of statutory interpretation known well to criminal lawyers, in dubio pro reo; if in doubt, then the interpretation is the one in favour of the accused. Then, Your Honour, I also pointed out that in Blagojevic, a decision of this Trial Chamber, paragraph 794, the Chamber said that "committing" means "committing." It doesn't mean these other forms of responsibility. So again, if the Prosecution is challenging what a Trial Chamber of this Tribunal has said, I would say it's fair enough that they have a burden to show that that is not a viable interpretation. Then, Your Honour, I went to all the Articles where "committing" appears in the Statute, and I said that "committing" there clearly means physically committing. And you may recall I said Article 1, which gives jurisdiction to the Tribunal, means committing because it has to be on the territory of Yugoslavia. If someone aids and abets a crime which is then committed in France or Germany, it's not within the competence of this Tribunal, and so "committing" means "committing." I then went to Article 7, I believe it is, or 9, territorial jurisdiction, where "committing" means "committing."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Enough --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And Article 2 as well, "committing or ordering to be committed" -- means always well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I -- the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: It was not my question that you repeat everything. My simple question was: Does the burden of proof rule only refer to questions of facts and evidence, or does it also refer to the question of interpretation? That was my very simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And I answered that, which is that the burden is on the Prosecution. It's a different burden. It's the burden of showing that a literal interpretation of the Statute is not -- is not a correct one. So its that burden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think -- I think it's a very incorrect use of the word "burden," because in matters of law, no one has a burden. In matters of law, it's a question of whether you succeed in convincing the Trial Chamber of the correct reading and sometimes interpretation of the law. These are submissions basically. No one has a burden of proving that a particular interpretation of the law is a correct one. You make your submissions, and the Trial Chamber will eventually decide whether they were convincing enough, whether we agree. They may be very convincing, and we may completely agree with you or the Prosecution in matters of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. May I just say this just in case the point then perhaps wasn't clear? It's the party which says that an Article should not be interpreted according to its plain words has maybe not a burden, an onus, but there's obviously something on them to say this word should not be interpreted as it appears. If someone says -- all right. That's fine. That's all I was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And ultimately, then there is this paradox surrounding this whole argument: that we may hear a submission from you or from the Prosecution on a particular legal issue and, as such, let's say it could be, in our minds, a very poor submission, but ultimately we ourselves can elaborate it further to the extent that what was initially a very poor submission on your part, one or the other, becomes a very strong, convincing argument which we will then apply in our decision. So this -- we're not speaking of burdens. I mean it's -- certainly you need not -- and no one was trying to confuse this issue as being amalgamated, being part and parcel or a horse-and-carriage relationship with the onus of proving facts and proving the guilt of the accused, which is almost absolute on the Prosecution in the sense that they have to prove it beyond reasonable doubt. Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just one sentence. But what has been said by the Presiding Judge is exactly what -- that was exactly my point. I just wanted to show some precedence against the inflationary use of the burden of proof rule, because it's really limited to certain issues. It doesn't cover the whole criminal law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's -- I understand, Ms. Sellers, that you wanted to address the Trial Chamber before we give the floor to the accused. Please be as brief as you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours. If I understand correctly, Mr. Oric will now be addressing the Trial Chamber under 84 bis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I never invited Mr. Oric to address the Trial Chamber under 84 bis. 84 bis relates to -- how I read it, to the initial stages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Fine. That is my first--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- of the proceedings. This is something different.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Fine. That's the first thing we did want to clarify, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And this morning I asked my learned friends would Mr. Oric being addressing the Chamber, and they told me that yes, he would be. That's when the Prosecution received notice on it. And we would like to put on the record, first, the clarification in terms of 84 bis. And then second is that not knowing that Mr. Oric was going to address the Trial Chamber, it came subsequent to your invitation, not knowing what would be the content or the gist of this address to the Trial Chamber, of course Prosecution did not take into account that in its submissions, particularly as it pertained to sentencing -- right. And we would just like to state what is probably the obvious, that this is an unsworn statement that has not been tested by the evidence. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's definitely an unsworn statement. It's definitely -- and I draw a parallel now from 84 bis under the statement "under the control of the Trial Chamber," and with the understanding that he is not being compelled to make a statement, and also with the understanding that neither we nor anyone else will ask him questions. Then as in the case of 84 bis but not pursuant to 84 bis, we will decide on the probative value of any statement that he may give, relevance or whatever weight we decide to attach to it. But the decision that we have taken is based on justice and not a particular -- a particular Rule. Certainly not 84 bis. Unfortunately, it seems that the -- while the Rules cover the opening stage of the trial, and while the Rules also provide, under 85, for any evidence on any relevant information that may assist the Trial Chamber in determining an appropriate sentence and that is regulated by evidence, when you come to the closing arguments - this is basically what we are basing it upon - the parties shall also address matters of sentencing and closing arguments, and on that basis we think that we should give the opportunity to the accused to have the final -- the final word before I declare the proceedings, the trial, closed pursuant to Rule 90 -- 97 or whatever it is. Yes. Mr. Oric, you have followed the debate these last few minutes. I understand that you wish to make a statement. I want you to confirm, first and foremost, that no one has compelled you to make this statement; in other words, that what you are about to tell us you will be telling us because you yourself, after consultation with your counsel, has decided to address us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I confirm that no one has forced me, and after consulting my lawyers, I wish to address to Your Honours. First --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Before you proceed, I also want to make sure that you are aware that anything that you may say will be considered by this Trial Chamber in its deliberations, or may be considered by this Trial Chamber in its deliberations even though it's not sworn evidence, even though it's freely being provided.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Oric, you may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, I wish to thank you for giving me the opportunity to address you. I will be very brief. Throughout the trial, I have listened very carefully to what my Defence counsel have said, and I have nothing to add to this. I trust Your Honours, and I trust that Your Honours will reach the right decision. I wish to thank all of you, and there is nothing further I wish to say. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you so much, Mr. Oric. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I suppose you have got no further submissions to make. So pursuant to Rule 87(A), which says: "When both parties have completed their presentation of the case, the Presiding Judge shall declare the hearing closed, and the Trial Chamber shall deliberate in private." The hearing is hereby declared closed, and we will be proceeding to deliberate in private. Our hope is that we will be able to hand down our final judgement end of June, the end of June. We will be doing our utmost to meet that target. You will, of course, be informed in due course by means of a Scheduling Order. I thank you so much for all your useful submissions both in the closing briefs but also the -- in the oral arguments that you have submitted. I can assure you that they will be of great assistance to us in our deliberations, which are -- this is not an easy case. So we will -- we do appreciate the contribution that you have made. Thank you so much, and you will see our faces again end of June. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: sine die. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.14 p.m.,
